vignette:
He is thirty-three years old, sitting at his drafting table in the small home studio he built two years ago. The afternoon light falls across a half-finished logo—a stylized tree for a local coffee roaster—but his eyes are not on the screen. They are fixed on the rearview mirror he never removed from the wall, angled just so that it catches the front door. He tells himself it helps him check the light.

The incident happened on a Saturday night, three years ago this coming autumn. He was driving home from a dinner with friends in the city, the kind of easy evening he used to take for granted. A traffic stop. Over a blown taillight, the officer said. He remembers the blue-red wash flooding his windshield, the click of his seatbelt releasing, the slow reach for his wallet. He did everything right. Hands on the wheel, movements deliberate, voice calm.

The officer ordered him out of the car. He remembers the slap of asphalt against his cheek before he understood he was on the ground. A knee drove into his back, pressing the air from his lungs. He heard his own voice saying please, and then the crack of his wrist snapping—a sound like a dry branch—as the officer wrenched his arm behind him. He never saw the face of the officer who broke him. Only the dark leather of a boot, the gravel digging into his cheek, the taste of blood and exhaust.

The charges were dropped. The police report called it a misunderstanding. The city settled for a modest sum. He signed a paper saying he would not speak of it again.

His body carries the memory differently. The wrist healed with a slight click when he rotates it—a sound he hears every time he picks up his stylus. He stopped driving after dark. Then he stopped driving at all. He sold his car sixth months after the incident, telling friends he wanted to bike more for his health. Now he walks everywhere, taking long, circuitous routes to avoid intersections where police cruisers park. One morning he crossed the street and a man in a blue jacket raised his arm to hail a cab; he must have ducked behind a parked van before he realized what he was doing. He stood there, heart hammering, eyes fixed on the empty curb, and felt a wave of shame so deep it made him nauseous.

The marriage cracked first. He began sleeping on the couch because the bedroom window faced the street. Every headlight sliding across the ceiling was a strobe. Every distant siren was the sound of a knee digging deeper. His wife tried to touch his shoulder one night and he swung at her, not knowing where he was, his hand stopping an inch from her face. He moved out three weeks later. The divorce was quiet, administrative. She left him a note that said, I don’t know who you are anymore. I wish I could have helped. He did not answer.

In his studio he works alone, taking only freelance commissions that require minimal client contact. He is good at what he does—focused, exact. But when the doorbell rings unexpectedly, his chest seizes. He waits, breath held, until the sound stops. He has stopped answering his phone. He has stopped checking the mail. He tells himself it is efficiency. He knows it is something else.

Some nights he sits in the dark with his laptop closed and scrolls through news articles about police shootings—officers cleared, families suing, body camera footage released. He reads until his eyes burn, looking for something he cannot name. A signal. A pattern. A reason the knee did not keep pressing.

He does not find it.

This morning he walked to the corner store for milk. A patrol car idled at the stop sign, engine purring. He turned around and went home. He has not eaten since yesterday. The draft of the coffee roaster logo sits untouched on the screen, its tree trunk a thin, steady line. He should finish it by tomorrow. He knows he will. But first he needs to check the front door again, just to be sure it is locked. Just to be sure no one is outside. Just to be sure.
